FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-1)(Part-12).p.text:
Functions 
- A function is a reusable block of JavaScript code designed to perform 
a particular task.  
- Instead of writing the same statements repeatedly, we can place 
them inside a function and call the function whenever required.  
- A function executes when it is called or invoked. 
Why Functions Are Used 
 To avoid repeating the same code. 
 To divide a large program into smaller tasks.  
 To improve code readability. 
 To make code easier to test and maintain. 
 To reuse the same logic with different values. 
Function Syntax 
function functionName(parameters) { 
    // statements 
} 
function is the keyword used to declare a function. functionName is the 
name given to the function. parameters are optional inputs received by the 
function. 
Function Declaration 
A function declaration defines a function using the function keyword.  
function greet() { 
    console.log("Hello Students"); 
} 
The above code only defines the function. The statements inside it execute 
when the function is called.

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-1)(Part-13).p.text:
JS Objects 
- JavaScript provides several built-in ways to store, organize, and work 
with data.  
- In this topic, we learn the commonly used JavaScript objects and 
object-like structures: Object, Array, String, Date, Math, Map, and 
Set. 
1. Object 
An object is a collection of related data stored as key -value pairs. Each key 
is called a property, and the value can contain data such as a string, 
number, Boolean, array, or another object. 
Creating an Object 
let student = { 
    name: "ABC", 
    age: 20, 
    course: "JavaScript" 
}; 
Accessing Object Properties 
Object properties can be accessed using dot notation or bracket notation.  
console.log(student.name); 
console.log(student["age"]); 
Output: 
ABC 
20 
Adding and Updating Properties 
student.city = "Vijayawada"; 
student.age = 21;

console.log(student.city); 
console.log(student.age); 
 A new property can be added using the object name and property 
name. 
 An existing property can be updated by assigning a new value.  
Deleting an Object Property 
delete student.city; 
The delete operator removes a property from an object.  
2. Array 
An array is an ordered collection of values. It is used when multiple values 
need to be stored under one variable. 
let marks = [80, 75, 90, 85]; 
Accessing Array Elements 
Array indexing starts from 0. 
console.log(marks[0]); 
console.log(marks[2]); 
Output: 
80 
90 
Common Array Properties and Methods 
Property / Method Purpose Example 
length Returns the number of elements. marks.length 
push() Adds an element at the end. marks.push(95) 
pop() Removes the last element. marks.pop() 
shift() Removes the first element. marks.shift() 
unshift() Adds an element at the 
beginning. marks.unshift(70)

3. String 
A string represents a sequence of characters or text. JavaScript provides 
several properties and methods for working with strings. 
let message = "Hello JavaScript"; 
Accessing String Characters 
console.log(message[0]); 
Output: H 
Common String Properties and Methods 
Property / 
Method 
Purpose Example 
length Returns the number 
of characters. 
message.length 
toUpperCase() Converts text to 
uppercase. 
message.toUpperCase() 
toLowerCase() Converts text to 
lowercase. 
message.toLowerCase() 
charAt() Returns the character 
at a position. 
message.charAt(0) 
includes() Checks whether text 
is present. 
message.includes("JavaScript") 
 
4. Date 
The Date object is used to work with dates and times in JavaScript.  
let currentDate = new Date(); 
console.log(currentDate); 
new Date() creates a Date object representing the current date and time.

Creating a Specific Date 
let date = new Date("2026-10-03"); 
console.log(date); 
Common Date Methods 
Method Purpose Example 
getFullYear() Returns the year. date.getFullYear() 
getMonth() Returns the month index. date.getMonth() 
getDate() Returns the day of the 
month. 
date.getDate() 
getDay() Returns the day of the week 
index. 
date.getDay() 
getHours() Returns the hour. date.getHours() 
getMinutes() Returns the minutes. date.getMinutes() 
 
Note: getMonth() returns a zero-based month index, where January is 0 
and December is 11. 
5. Math 
Math is a built -in JavaScript object that provides mathematical constants 
and methods. It is used for common mathematical calculations.  
console.log(Math.PI); 
console.log(Math.sqrt(25)); 
console.log(Math.pow(2, 3)); 
Output: 
3.141592653589793 
5 
8 
Common Math Properties and Methods 
Property / Method Purpose Example 
Math.PI Returns the value of π. Math.PI

Math.sqrt() Returns the square root. Math.sqrt(25) 
Math.pow() Returns a number raised to a 
power. 
Math.pow(2, 3) 
Math.round() Rounds to the nearest integer. Math.round(4.6) 
Math.floor() Rounds down. Math.floor(4.9) 
Math.ceil() Rounds up. Math.ceil(4.1) 
Math.max() Returns the largest value. Math.max(10, 
20, 30) 
Math.min() Returns the smallest value. Math.min(10, 
20, 30) 
Math.random() Returns a random number from 0 
up to, but not including, 1. 
Math.random() 
 
6. Map 
A Map is a collection of key -value pairs. Unlike a regular object, a Map can 
use different types of values as keys. 
let student = new Map(); 
 
student.set("name", "ABC"); 
student.set("age", 20); 
 
console.log(student.get("name")); 
console.log(student.get("age")); 
Output: 
ABC 
20 
Common Map Methods 
Method Purpose Example 
set() Adds or updates a key-value pair. student.set("age", 21) 
get() Returns the value for a key. student.get("age") 
has() Checks whether a key exists. student.has("name")

delete() Removes a key-value pair. student.delete("age") 
clear() Removes all key-value pairs. student.clear() 
size Returns the number of entries. student.size 
 
7. Set 
A Set is a collection of unique values. Duplicate values are automatically 
ignored. 
let numbers = new Set(); 
 
numbers.add(10); 
numbers.add(20); 
numbers.add(10); 
 
console.log(numbers); 
The value 10 is stored only once because a Set does not allow duplicate 
values. 
Common Set Methods 
Method Purpose Example 
add() Adds a value. numbers.add(30) 
has() Checks whether a value exists. numbers.has(20) 
delete() Removes a value. numbers.delete(20) 
clear() Removes all values. numbers.clear() 
size Returns the number of unique 
values. 
numbers.size

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-1)(Part-14).p.text:
Browser Object Model (BOM) 
- The Browser Object Model (BOM) allows JavaScript to interact with 
the web browser. It provides objects that represent the browser 
window and browser-related information. 
- BOM is used to working with the browser window. 
- It provides information about the current URL, browser, screen, and 
browsing history. 
- The window object is the main object of the BOM.  
BOM Structure 
window 
    ├── location 
    ├── history 
    ├── navigator 
    ├── screen 
The window object represents the brow ser window. Other browser -related 
objects can be accessed through window. 
1. Window Object 
The window object represents the browser window in which the web page 
is displayed. It is the top-level object available in browser-side JavaScript. 
window.alert("Welcome"); 
In many cases, window can be omitted. 
alert("Welcome"); 
Common Window Properties 
Property Purpose 
innerWidth Returns the width of the browser's content area.  
innerHeight Returns the height of the browser's content area.

console.log(window.innerWidth); 
console.log(window.innerHeight); 
Common Window Methods 
Method Purpose 
alert() Displays a message box. 
confirm() Displays OK and Cancel buttons. 
prompt() Accepts input from the user. 
open() Opens a new browser window or tab. 
close() Attempts to close a window opened by script. 
 
alert() 
The alert() method displays a message to the user.  
alert("Welcome to JavaScript"); 
confirm() 
The confirm() method displays a dialog box with OK and Cancel buttons. It 
returns true when OK is selected and false when Cancel is selected. 
let result = confirm("Do you want to continue?"); 
console.log(result); 
prompt() 
The prompt() method displays a dialog box that allows the user to enter a 
value. 
let name = prompt("Enter your name"); 
console.log(name); 
2. Location Object 
The location object contains information about the current page URL and 
can be used to navigate to another page.

console.log(window.location.href); 
Common Location Properties 
Property Purpose 
href Returns the complete URL. 
hostname Returns the domain name. 
pathname Returns the path of the current page. 
protocol Returns the URL protocol. 
 
Common Location Methods 
Method Purpose 
assign() Loads another page. 
reload() Reloads the current page. 
replace() Loads another page and replaces the current history entry. 
 
location.assign("https://example.com"); 
location.reload(); 
3. History Object 
It represents the pages visited in the current browser session. It can be 
used to move backward or forward through the browsing history.  
Common History Methods 
Method Purpose 
back() Moves to the previous page. 
forward() Moves to the next page. 
go() Moves to a particular position in the session history.  
 
history.back(); 
history.forward(); 
history.go(-1); 
history.go(-1) moves one page backward in the session history.

4. Navigator Object 
The navigator object provides information about the browser and its 
environment. 
Common Navigator Properties 
Property Purpose 
userAgent Returns information about the browser's user-agent 
string. 
language Returns the browser's preferred language. 
onLine Indicates whether the browser reports that it is online.  
 
console.log(navigator.userAgent); 
console.log(navigator.language); 
console.log(navigator.onLine); 
Note: Browser identification should not normally rely only on userAgent 
because its value can vary or be modified. 
5. Screen Object 
The screen object provides information about the user's screen.  
Common Screen Properties 
Property Purpose 
width Returns the screen width in CSS pixels. 
height Returns the screen height in CSS pixels. 
availWidth Returns the available screen width. 
availHeight Returns the available screen height. 
colorDepth Returns the color depth of the screen. 
 
console.log(screen.width); 
console.log(screen.height);

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-1)(Part-15).p.text:
Document Object Model (DOM) 
- The Document Object Model (DOM) represents an HTML page as a 
document that JavaScript can access and modify.  
- JavaScript can use the DOM to read HTML content.  
- JavaScript can change the content of HTML elements.  
- JavaScript can create dynamic changes in a web page. 
- The document object is used to work with the HTML document.  
DOM Methods and Properties 
The following methods and properties are important for basic DOM 
programming. 
Methods 
1. document.write() 
The document.write() meth od writes content directly into the HTML 
document. 
document.write("Hello Students"); 
Output: Hello Students 
2. document.writeln() 
The document.writeln() method writes text to the document and adds a 
newline character after the text. 
document.writeln("Hello"); 
document.writeln("Students"); 
The method is similar to document.write(), but it writes a newline after the 
supplied text. 
3. document.getElementById() 
The getElementById() method finds an HTML element using its id attribute.

Hello

The method returns the element whose id matches the supplied value. Changing an Element Using getElementById()

Old Message

The content of the paragraph changes from Old Message to New Message. 4. document.getElementsByClassName() The getElementsByClassName() method finds HTML elements that have a specified class name.

One

Two

The method returns to a collection of elements that have the specified class. 5. document.getElementsByTagName() The getElementsByTagName() method finds HTML elements using their tag name, such as p, h1, div, or li.

First Paragraph

Second Paragraph

The method returns to a collection containing all matching elements. Note Name Main Purpose document.write() Writes content to the document. document.writeln() Writes content with a newline. document.getElementById() Finds an element using its id. document.getElementsByClassName() Finds elements using a class name. document.getElementsByTagName() Finds elements using a tag name. Properties Properties are used to read or change information associated with an HTML element. 1. innerHTML The innerHTML property gets or changes the HTML content inside an element.

Hello

The content inside the paragraph becomes bold because HTML markup is interpreted.

Reading innerHTML let content = document.getElementById("message").innerHTML; console.log(content); innerHTML can read the HTML markup contained inside an element. 2. innerText The innerText property gets or changes the visible text inside an element.

Hello Students

The visible text changes to Welcome Students. innerHTML vs innerText Property Purpose Example innerHTML Gets or sets HTML content inside an element. element.innerHTML = "Hello"; innerText Gets or sets visible text inside an element. element.innerText = "Hello";

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-1)(Part-17).p.text:
ES6 Features 
- ES6 stands for ECMAScript 6 and is also known as ECMAScript 2015. 
It is a major version of JavaScript that introduced features designed 
to make JavaScript code shorter, cleaner, and easier to maintain.  
ES6 Features  
Feature Main Idea 
let and const Modern variable declarations 
Arrow Functions Short function syntax 
Template Literals Strings with variables and expressions 
Destructuring Extract values from arrays and objects 
Default Parameters Default function arguments 
Rest and Spread Collect and expand values 
Classes Blueprint for objects 
Modules Share and reuse code 
for...of Iterate through values 
Map Key-value collection 
Set Unique-value collection 
 
1. let and const 
ES6 introduced let and const for declaring variables. Both are  block-scoped. 
let age = 25; 
age = 30; 
const name = "ABC"; 
console.log(age); 
console.log(name); 
Output: 
30  ABC 
 let → the value can be reassigned. 
 const → the variable cannot be reassigned. 
 Both are block-scoped.

 They are generally preferred over var in modern JavaScript. 
Remember: let → can change | const → cannot be reassigned  
2. Arrow Functions 
Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax for writing functions.  
const add = (a, b) => a + b; 
 
console.log(add(10, 20)); 
Output: 30 
 Uses the => syntax. 
 Makes function expressions shorter. 
 Commonly used with arrays and callbacks. 
 Arrow functions have lexical this behavior. 
Remember: Arrow Function → Shorter way to write a function  
3. Template Literals 
Template literals make it easy to create strings containing variables and 
expressions. 
let name = "ABC"; 
let age = 20; 
 
console.log(`Name: ${name}, Age: ${age}`); 
Output: Name: ABC, Age: 20 
 Uses backticks (` `). 
 Use ${} to insert variables or expressions. 
 Reduces string concatenation using +. 
Remember: Template Literal → String + variables/expressions using 
backticks

Output: ABC 
 set() adds or updates a key-value pair. 
 get() retrieves a value using its key. 
 Map can use different types of values as keys. 
Remember: Map → Key-value pairs 
11. Set 
Set is a collection that stores unique values. 
let numbers = new Set(); 
 
numbers.add(10); 
numbers.add(20); 
numbers.add(10); 
 
console.log(numbers); 
The duplicate value 10 is stored only once. 
 add() adds a value. 
 has() checks whether a value exists. 
 Set does not store duplicate values. 
Remember: Set → Unique values

GIT 
List of Topics 
1. Introduction to VCS and GIT  
2. GIT Installation  
3. GITHUB Account Creation

6. Working with Branches

Introduction to Version Control System (VCS) 
- A Version Control System (VCS) is a software tool used to track changes made to 
files and source code over time.  
- It helps developers maintain different versions of a project and understand what 
changes were made. 
- VCS is especially useful when multiple developers work on the same project 
because it helps them manage changes, collaborate, and recover earlier versions 
when required. 
Why Version Control is Needed 
Without version control, developers may create many copies of the same project, such 
as: 
 project_final 
 project_final_new 
 project_final_latest 
This approach makes it difficult to identify which version is correct and who made a 
particular change. 
A VCS provides a systematic way to: 
 Track changes in source code. 
 Maintain the history of a project.

 Identify who made a change. 
 Restore an earlier version when required. 
 Allow multiple developers to work on the same project.  
 Create separate development paths using branches.  
Types of Version Control Systems 
Type Description Example 
Local VCS Version history is maintained on the local 
computer. RCS 
Centralized VCS A central server stores the main version history.  SVN 
Distributed VCS Each developer can have a complete repository 
with its history. GIT 
 
What is GIT 
- GIT is a distributed version control system used to track changes in source code 
and manage different versions of a project. 
- GIT was originally created by Linus Torvalds in 2005  
- GIT is commonly used with platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket for 
remote repository hosting and collaboration. (GitHub is preferable) 
Why is GIT Used 
 To maintain the history of source-code changes. 
 To work on different features separately using branches.  
 To compare changes between versions. 
 To restore previous versions of files. 
 To support collaboration between developers. 
 To work locally and synchronize changes with remote repositories.  
Features of GIT 
 Distributed – Each developer can have a complete local repository.  
 Version History – Changes can be recorded and reviewed.  
 Branching – Developers can create separate branches for features or fixes.  
 Merging – Changes from different branches can be combined.  
 Collaboration – Multiple developers can work on the same project.  
 Data Integrity – GIT uses checksums to identify and protect stored c ontent.

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-2)(Part-2).pd.text:
GIT Installation 
- Before using GIT commands, GIT must be installed on the computer. After 
installation, the GIT command can be used from a terminal or command prompt.  
What is GIT Installation 
GIT Installation is the process of installing the GIT software on a computer so that GIT 
commands can be executed and repositories can be managed.  
Installing GIT on Windows 
The basic installation steps are: 
1. Open a web browser. 
2. Go to the official GIT website. 
3. Download the GIT installer for Windows.  
4. Run the downloaded installer. 
5. Follow the installation wizard. 
6. Keep the default options unless a specific configuration is required.  
7. Complete the installation. 
Verify GIT Installation 
After installation, open Command Prompt, PowerShell, Git Bash, or another terminal 
and execute: 
git --version 
        If GIT is installed correctly, the command displays the installed GIT version.  
git version 2.x.x 
The exact version number depends on the version installed on the computer.  
 
GitHub Account Creation 
- GitHub is a platform used to host GIT repositories and support software-
development collaboration. A GitHub account allows a user to create and 
manage repositories on GitHub. 
GIT and GitHub 
GIT GitHub 
Version control software Online platform for hosting and collaborating GIT 
repositories.

Runs on the developer's 
computer. 
Provides repositories and collaboration features through 
an online service. 
Tracks changes and 
creates commits. Can store and share repositories remotely.  
Steps to Create a GitHub Account 
1. Open a web browser. 
2. Go to the official GitHub website. 
3. Select the option to create a new account.  
4. Enter the required email address. 
5. Create a password. 
6. Choose a GitHub username. 
7. Complete the required verification steps.  
8. Verify the email address if requested. 
9. Complete the account setup. 
Choosing a GitHub Username 
A username identifies the user's GitHub account and appears in the user's GitHub 
profile and repository URLs. 
 Choose a professional and easy-to-remember username. 
 Avoid unnecessarily complicated names.  
 Remember that the username can become part of repository links.  
GitHub Repository 
A repository on GitHub is an online location where a project's files and GIT history can 
be stored. 
For example, a student may create a repository named:  
student-management-project 
 
GIT Configuration 
- After installing GIT, basic configuration should be performed before creating 
commits. The most important configuration is the user's name and email 
address.

Why GIT Configuration is Needed 
- GIT records the author information along with commits. Configuring the user 
name and email helps identify who created a particular commit.  
Check Existing Configuration 
To display the current GIT configuration, use:  
git config --list 
To check the configured user name:  
git config user.name 
To check the configured email: 
git config user.email 
Configure User Name 
Use the following command: 
git config --global user.name "Your Name"  
Configure Email 
Use the following command: 
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"  
The --global option applies the configuration to the user's GIT configuration for 
repositories on that computer. 
Example 
git config --global user.name "abc" 
git config --global user.email "abc@gmail.com"  
Verify Configuration 
After configuring the name and email, verify them using: 
git config --global user.name 
git config --global user.email 
 
Local Repository Configuration 
GIT also allows configuration to be applied only to a particular repository. This is useful 
when a repository needs settings different from the global configuration. 
git config user.name "Project User"

git config user.email "project@example.com"  
 
A repository-specific configuration takes precedence over the corresponding global 
setting for that repository. 
Global vs Local Configuration 
Configuration Scope Command Example 
Global Applies to repositories for the 
current user on the computer. 
git config --global user.name 
"Your Name" 
Local Applies only to the current 
repository. 
git config user.name "Project 
User" 
Useful GIT Configuration Commands 
Command Purpose 
git config --list Displays configuration settings. 
git config user.name Displays the name configured for the current 
repository. 
git config user.email Displays the email configured for the current 
repository. 
git config --global user.name "Name" Sets the global user name. 
git config --global user.email "Email" Sets the global email.

FEDF LEcture Notes (Module-2)(Part-3).pd.text:
GIT Basics 
- GIT Basics covers the fundamental commands required to start working with a 
project using GIT. These commands help a developer create a repository, check 
file status, prepare changes, save changes as commits, and view the history of 
committed changes. 
1. GIT Installation 
Command 
git --version 
Purpose of the Command 
- Check whether GIT is installed and displays the installed GIT version.  
Example 
git --version 
 
Example output: 
git version 2.x.x 
 
2. GIT Configuration 
Command 
git config --global user.name "Your Name" 
git config --global user.email "your@email.com" 
Purpose of the Command 
- Configures the name and email associated with commits.  
Example 
git config --global user.name "Rahul Kumar" 
git config --global user.email "rahul@example.com" 
 
3. GIT Initialization 
Command 
git init

Purpose of the Command 
- Creates a new local GIT repository in the current project folder.  
Example 
cd StudentManagement 
git init 
 
4. GIT Status 
Command 
git status 
Purpose of the Command 
- Shows the current state of the working directory and staging area. 
Example 
git status 
 
5. GIT Staging 
Staging selects changes that should be included in the next commit. The staging area is 
between the working directory and the repository.  
A. Adding a Single File 
Command 
                   git add Student.java 
           Purpose 
                   Stages only Student.java. 
B. Adding Multiple Files 
Command 
           git add Student.java Course.java 
            Purpose 
                   Stages the specified files.

C. Adding All Files 
          Command 
                     git add . 
           Purpose  
                   Stages all applicable changes in the current directory and its subdirectories.  
 
6. GIT Commit 
Command 
git commit -m "Commit message" 
Purpose of the Command 
- Records the currently staged changes in the local repository.  
Example 
git commit -m "Added student class" 
 
7. GIT Commit History 
Detailed History 
Command 
git log 
Purpose of the Command 
- Displays the commit history of the current repository.  
Example 
git log 
Short History 
Command 
git log --oneline 
Purpose 
        Displays each commit in a compact single-line format.

GIT Basics – Command Summary 
Command Purpose 
git --version Checks installed GIT version. 
git config Configures GIT settings. 
git init Creates a local GIT repository. 
git status Shows repository/worktree state. 
git add <file> Stages one file. 
git add file1 file2 Stages selected files. 
git add . Stages all applicable changes. 
git commit -m Records staged changes. 
git log Shows detailed history. 
git log --oneline Shows compact history.

FEDF Lecture Notes (Module-2)(Part-4).pd.text:
Working with Branches 
- GIT branch is a separate line of development in a repository. Branches allow 
developers to work on features, fixes, or experiments without directly changing the 
main development line. 
- A branch can be created from an existing point in the project's history. Developers 
can work on the branch, create commits, and later merge the changes into another 
branch. 
Why Branches are Used 
 To develop new features separately.  
 To fix bugs without disturbing the main development line.  
 To allow multiple developers to work on different tasks.  
 To test or experiment with changes safely.  
 To organize project development.  
 To combine completed work using merging.  
Understanding the Main Branch 
The main branch is commonly used as the primary branch of a repository. Depending 
on the repository or project, it may be named main or another name.  
The important idea is that developers can create separate branches from the main 
development line and work independently.  
main 
  | 
  +------ feature-login 
  | 
  +------ feature-payment 
 
Checking the Current Branch 
Command 
git branch 
Purpose of the Command 
- The git branch command displays local branches. The current branch is normally 
indicated with an asterisk (*). 
Example

git branch 
 
* main 
  feature-login 
  feature-payment 
In this example, the asterisk indicates that main is the current branch.  
 
Creating a New Branch 
Command 
git branch feature-login 
Purpose of the Command 
- Creates a new branch named feature-login without automatically switching to it. 
Example 
git branch feature-login 
git branch 
 
After creation, the new branch appears in the branch list, but the current branch 
remains unchanged. 
Switching to a Branch 
Command 
git switch feature-login 
Purpose of the Command 
- Switches the working directory to the specified existing branch.  
Example 
git switch feature-login 
git branch 
 
The asterisk now appears next to feature-login. 
 
Creating and Switching to a Branch

Command 
git switch -c feature-login 
Purpose of the Command 
- Creates a new branch and switches to it in one command.  
Example 
git switch -c feature-login 
git branch 
 
This is a convenient command when starting work on a new feature.  
Note: Alternative Command 
  git checkout -b feature-login 
This older command can also create and switch to a branch. For new classroom 
examples, git switch is clearer because it is specifically designed for branch switching.  
 
Viewing Branches 
Local Branches 
git branch 
        Purpose: Displays local branches.  
Branches with More Information 
git branch -v 
        Purpose: Displays local branches with information about their latest    commits.  
 
Working with a Branch 
Once a developer switches to a branch, changes can be made and committed normally.  
git switch feature-login 
 
# Modify project files 
 
git status 
git add . 
git commit -m "Added login feature"

The commit is created on the current branch. The main branch is not automatically 
updated by this commit. 
Note: Branch and Commit Relationship 
Each branch points to a line of commits. When a new commit is created on a branch, 
that branch moves forward to include the new commit.  
main 
A --- B 
 
feature-login 
A --- B --- C --- D 
Here, commits C and D belong to the feature-login development line. The main branch 
still points to B until the feature branch is merged. 
 
Merging Branches 
Merging is the process of combining changes from one branch into another branch.  
Basic Workflow 
git switch main 
git merge feature-login 
Purpose of git merge 
The git merge command combines the changes from the specified branch into the 
currently switched branch. 
Example 
git switch main 
git merge feature-login 
 
Here, feature-login is merged into main. The developer must first switch to the branch 
that should receive the changes. 
Note: 
 The branch being merged into is the current branch.  
 The branch named in git merge is the source of the changes.  
 After a successful merge, the changes from the source branch become part of the 
target branch.

Renaming a Branch 
Command 
git branch -m old-name new-name 
Purpose of the Command 
        Renames a local branch. 
Example 
git branch -m feature-login login-feature 
 
Deleting a Branch 
Command 
git branch -d feature-login 
Purpose of the Command 
- Deletes the specified local branch when its changes have been merged or Git 
considers it safe to delete. 
Example 
git switch main 
git branch -d feature-login 
 
A branch should normally be deleted after its work has been merged and is no longer 
required. 
Note: Force Deleting a Branch 
git branch -D feature-login 
 
Purpose: Force deletes the local branch. This should be used carefully because it can 
remove a branch that contains unmerged work.

Remote Repository 
- A remote repository is a GIT repository stored on another system or on an online 
repository hosting platform. It allows developers to store, share, and 
synchronize project history with other developers.  
 
- A local repository is stored on the developer's computer, while a remote 
repository is stored separately and can be accessed through a network.  
Local Repository vs Remote Repository 
Local Repository Remote Repository 
Stored on the developer's computer. Stored on another system or repository 
hosting platform. 
Can be used without continuously 
connecting to a network. 
Usually accessed through a network 
connection. 
Contains project files and GIT history.  Can contain a shared copy of project files 
and GIT history. 
Used for local development and commits. Used for sharing and synchronizing work.  
Why Remote Repositories are Used 
 To store a shared copy of a project.  
 To back up project history outside the local computer.  
 To share code with other developers. 
 To synchronize work between developers. 
 To support collaboration using branches and commits.  
 To make a project accessible from multiple development environments.  
Understanding Remote 
A remote is a reference or name that represents a remote repository. The commonly 
used default remote name is origin. 
origin  →  Remote Repository  
The name origin is only a convenient name. A different remote name can also be used.  
Connecting a Local Repository to a Remote Repository 
Before pushing local commits to a remote repository, a local repository must be 
connected to the remote repository.

Basic Workflow 
Local Repository 
      ↓ 
Add Remote 
      ↓ 
Remote Repository 
      ↓ 
Push Changes 
 
Adding a Remote Repository 
Command 
git remote add origin <repository-url> 
Purpose of the Command 
- Adds a remote repository and gives it the name origin.  
Example 
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/student-
management.git 
Here, origin is the remote name, and the URL identifies the remote repository.  
Note 
 The URL must point to the intended remote repository. 
 The remote name origin is commonly used, but it is not mandatory.  
 
Viewing Remote Repositories 
Command 
git remote -v 
Purpose of the Command 
- Displays the configured remote repository names and their URLs.  
Example 
git remote -v

origin  https://github.com/username/student-management.git 
(fetch) 
origin  https://github.com/username/student-management.git 
(push) 
 
Pushing Changes to a Remote Repository 
Command 
git push origin main 
Purpose of the Command 
- Sends local commits from the specified branch to the specified remote 
repository. 
Example 
git switch main 
git push origin main 
Here, origin is the remote name and main is the branch being pushed.  
 
Pulling Changes from a Remote Repository  
Command 
git pull 
Purpose of the Command 
- Gets changes from the configured remote tracking branch and integrates them 
into the current local branch. 
Example 
git switch main 
git pull 
This is commonly used when the remote repository contains changes that are not yet 
present in the local branch.

Fetching Changes from a Remote Repository 
Command 
git fetch 
Purpose of the Command 
- Download new data and updates remote-tracking information without 
automatically integrating the changes into the current working branch.  
Example 
git fetch 
git status 
Fetch is useful when a developer wants to inspect remote changes before deciding 
how to integrate them. 
 
Cloning a Remote Repository 
Command 
git clone <repository-url> 
Purpose of the Command 
- Creates a local copy of an existing remote repository, including its project files 
and GIT history. 
Example 
git clone https://github.com/username/student-management.git 
A new local project directory is created from the remote repository.
